title: SHE CAME TO EXPOSE A KING WITH QUESTIONS—BUT WHAT SHE DISCOVERED LEFT HER SPEECHLESS
paragraphs: SHE CAME TO EXPOSE A KING WITH QUESTIONS—BUT WHAT SHE DISCOVERED LEFT HER SPEECHLESS

The Queen of Sheba traveled across dangerous distances to test Solomon’s wisdom. She expected extraordinary answers. What she encountered was something far greater—and 3,000 years later, her story still confronts everyone searching for truth, carrying unanswered questions, or wondering whether God is really who He says He is.
“And when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to prove him with hard questions.” — 1 Kings 10:1 (KJV)
She did not travel all that distance because she was easily impressed.
She was a queen.
She had wealth. Influence. Authority. Resources. People who answered when she called. Servants who attended to her needs. An entire kingdom accustomed to her commands.
But there was something she did not possess.
An answer to every question.
And somewhere beyond the borders of her kingdom, a rumor had reached her ears.
There was a king in Jerusalem whose wisdom was unlike anything the world had seen.
Not merely a man who could speak beautifully.
Not simply a ruler surrounded by gold.
A king whose understanding had become so extraordinary that his reputation was connected to the name of the LORD.
And the queen wanted to know whether the stories were true.
So she prepared a journey.
Camels carrying spices. Precious stones. Gold. An impressive royal procession crossing the ancient world.
But the most important thing she carried was invisible.
Questions.
Questions difficult enough to test a king.
Questions that wealth could not answer.
Questions that required something deeper than intelligence.
And perhaps that is where her story begins to sound strangely familiar.
Because you may not have a crown.
You may not command an army.
You may not own gold or precious stones.
But you know what it means to carry questions that refuse to leave you alone.
Why did God allow that loss?
Why did the person you trusted betray you?
Why does obedience sometimes feel harder than rebellion?
Why do people who ignore God appear to prosper while those trying to follow Him struggle?
Why does heaven sometimes seem silent when your heart is screaming?
And perhaps the question you have been afraid to say aloud:
“Lord, if You are really with me, why does my life look like this?”
The Queen of Sheba came with hard questions.
And Scripture tells us something remarkable.
Solomon did not dismiss them.
He did not shame her for asking.
He did not demand that she pretend to understand.
First Kings 10:2 says she came to Solomon and communed with him of all that was in her heart.
Read that again.
All that was in her heart.
The Hebrew expression is כָּל־אֲשֶׁר הָיָה עִם־לְבָבָהּ (kol-asher hayah im-levavah), expressing everything that was in her heart.
This was more than a ceremonial exchange between rulers.
She brought what she had been carrying within.
And Solomon listened.
There is something deeply moving about that.
Because many people have spent years sitting in churches while secretly believing their questions make them unworthy of belonging there.
They smile during worship.
They say amen.
They post Bible verses.
But beneath the surface, their faith is wrestling with things they are terrified to confess.
They fear that asking difficult questions means they are doubting God.
Yet the Bible does not hide the struggles of people who sought Him.
David cried out in anguish.
Job wrestled with suffering.
Habakkuk questioned the violence and injustice around him.
Thomas struggled to believe the resurrection testimony.
And the father of a suffering child cried to Jesus:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.” — Mark 9:24 (KJV)
God's Word does not teach us to celebrate unbelief.
But it does show us that honest questions can become the beginning of a deeper search for truth.
The danger is not always that you have questions.
Sometimes the danger is that you have stopped bringing them to God.
You have allowed disappointment to become distance.
You have allowed pain to become suspicion.
You have allowed unanswered prayers to become a reason to abandon the One who alone can give eternal life.
And slowly, without realizing it, you have begun treating your wounds as greater authorities than His Word.
But the Queen of Sheba did something many people never do.
She went searching.
She refused to settle for secondhand reports.
She wanted to see whether what she had heard was true.
And when she arrived in Jerusalem, the answers were only the beginning.
First Kings 10:3 declares:
“And Solomon told her all her questions: there was not any thing hid from the king, which he told her not.” (KJV)
Every question she presented received an answer.
But then something happened that no amount of preparation could have anticipated.
She looked around.
She saw Solomon's wisdom.
She saw the house he had built.
She saw the food at his table.
She saw the organization of his servants, the attendance of his ministers, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up to the house of the LORD.
And Scripture records an extraordinary reaction.
“There was no more spirit in her.” — 1 Kings 10:5 (KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
וְלֹא־הָיָה בָהּ עוֹד רוּחַ
Ve-lo hayah vah od ruach.
Literally, there was no more breath or spirit in her.
The expression communicates overwhelming astonishment.
She was left breathless.
Not because she had seen something imaginary.
Not because someone had manipulated her emotions.
But because the reality before her exceeded the reports she had received.
She had heard about Solomon's wisdom.
Now she had witnessed it.
She had heard about the greatness of his kingdom.
Now she stood inside it.
And what she saw surpassed what she had believed.
Listen to her own words:
“Behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard.” — 1 Kings 10:7 (KJV)
The half was not told me.
Imagine the weight of that confession.
A powerful queen who had traveled from afar suddenly realized that everything she had heard had been an understatement.
But the most important moment of this story is not her amazement at Solomon.
It is what she said next.

“Blessed be the LORD thy God, which delighted in thee, to set thee on the throne of Israel: because the LORD loved Israel for ever, therefore made he thee king, to do judgment and justice.” — 1 Kings 10:9 (KJV)
She recognized that Solomon's wisdom and royal position were connected to the LORD's favor and purpose for Israel.
Notice where her praise went.
Beyond the gold.
Beyond the palace.
Beyond the impressive servants.
Beyond the king himself.
To the LORD.
That is the moment this story becomes far more than a historical account of royal splendor.
Because genuine God-given wisdom should never terminate in admiration of the person who possesses it.
It should direct attention toward the God who gives it.
And here is where we must be careful.
Solomon's kingdom was magnificent, but Solomon was not the Savior.
His wisdom was a gift, but he was not the source of all wisdom.
His reign displayed extraordinary blessing, but his heart would later be led astray.
First Kings 11 records a devastating turn.
The same Solomon who once asked God for wisdom eventually allowed his many foreign wives to turn his heart after other gods.
The king whose wisdom astonished a queen failed to remain wholly devoted to the LORD.
Think about that.
A man can possess extraordinary wisdom and still make devastatingly foolish choices when he stops obeying God.
A person can know Scripture and still resist surrender.
A person can teach truth and still tolerate hidden compromise.
A person can impress a crowd while quietly drifting away from the God he claims to serve.
That should sober every one of us.
Because the tragedy of Solomon's later years reminds us that knowledge alone cannot save a human soul.
Religious reputation cannot save us.
Public success cannot save us.
Even extraordinary spiritual privileges cannot replace faithful obedience.
And this is where the story begins to turn toward Someone greater.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ spoke about the Queen of Sheba.
He did not treat her journey as a meaningless legend.
He used her response to confront a generation that was demanding signs while refusing to recognize the truth standing before them.
In Matthew 12:42, Jesus said:

“The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon is here.” (KJV)
A GREATER THAN SOLOMON IS HERE.
Do you understand the weight of those words?
The Queen of Sheba traveled an extraordinary distance to hear the wisdom of a human king.
But the people standing before Jesus were encountering One greater than that king.
Solomon received wisdom from God.
Jesus is the eternal Son of God, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).
Solomon ruled an earthly kingdom.
Jesus is the promised Messiah whose kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:32–33).
Solomon's obedience eventually failed.
Jesus obeyed the Father perfectly, even unto death (Philippians 2:8).
Solomon could answer difficult questions.
Jesus came to deal with humanity's deepest problem.
Sin.
The Queen of Sheba was astonished by the greatness of Solomon.
But the Gospel reveals a King whose greatness is displayed not merely through royal splendor, but through humility, sacrifice, resurrection, and saving grace.
The King of kings entered a broken world.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He showed compassion to the weary.
He spoke truth that exposed hidden hearts.
He endured rejection, betrayal, mockery, and crucifixion.
And He did not go to the cross because humanity had become worthy of His sacrifice.
He went because sinners desperately needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we stopped struggling.
Not after we finally became impressive enough to approach Him.
While we were sinners.
That is grace.
And it changes everything.
Because perhaps you have been approaching God the way the Queen of Sheba approached Solomon.
You have heard the reports.
You have heard people testify about forgiveness.
You have watched others speak about peace.
You have seen lives transformed.
But deep inside, you are still wondering whether what you have heard could ever become real for you.
Could Jesus forgive what you did?
Could He receive someone who has fallen so many times?
Could He restore a person who has wasted years?
Could He save someone who has spent most of life running from Him?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that you are good enough to climb your way to God. It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says salvation is by grace through faith, not of works.
And the invitation of Christ remains:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
Not everyone who comes to Christ receives an immediate explanation for every painful event.
The Bible does not promise that.
Some questions remain unanswered in this life.
Some grief must be carried through seasons of patient trust.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
But Jesus offers something greater than the illusion of controlling every outcome.
He offers Himself.
His forgiveness.
His presence.
His truth.
His eternal life.
And His promise that those who come to Him in faith will not be cast out (John 6:37).
That is why this account should confront both the skeptic and the believer.
To the skeptic, it asks:
You have heard things about Jesus. But have you seriously examined who He claimed to be, what He taught, and what His death and resurrection mean?
To the believer, it asks something equally searching:
You already know the name of Jesus. But are you actually following Him?
Because there is a frightening difference between being familiar with Christ and being surrendered to Christ.
You can know the language of Christianity while refusing the Lordship of Jesus.
You can admire His teachings while resisting His commands.
You can share Scripture publicly while privately making peace with sin.
You can spend years near Christian things without cultivating a life of repentance, prayer, obedience, and love.
And sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not open rebellion.
It is comfortable familiarity.
You hear another sermon.
Another Bible verse.
Another warning.
Another invitation to return.
And you tell yourself there will be time tomorrow.
But tomorrow is not promised.
The Queen of Sheba responded to what she had heard by making the journey.
And Jesus, the greater King, calls us not merely to admire His wisdom but to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in Mark 1:15 is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite).
It calls for repentance—a genuine turning of mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because your sin was discovered.
It is not merely crying because your choices have consequences.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And true faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting Him as Savior and Lord.
That does not mean Christians become instantly flawless.
It means grace does not leave us content to remain enslaved to what Christ came to deliver us from.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live in a way that honors Him.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
And this is why our message has always carried such weight:
Not because the past becomes imaginary.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because every damaged relationship is automatically restored.
But because Jesus can redeem a life that sin has devastated.
He can forgive the guilty.
He can humble the proud.
He can restore hope to the ashamed.
He can give a new identity to those who have been defined by their worst decisions.
And He can turn a testimony of rebellion into a testimony of mercy.
Perhaps the scandal in your life is something other people know about.
Or perhaps it is something nobody has ever discovered.
The secret addiction.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The dishonesty that has become normal.
The relationship you know is drawing you away from God.
The spiritual pride that allows you to condemn others while excusing yourself.
The quiet refusal to forgive.
The faith you display in public but neglect in private.
Whatever it is, hiding it does not heal it.
Jesus already knows the truth.
And His call is not to continue pretending.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not permission to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to stop defending what is destroying you.
You do not have to manufacture a flawless testimony before coming to Christ.
You come because you need His mercy.
And maybe that is the hardest question of all.
Not whether God can forgive you.
But whether you are willing to stop running from the forgiveness He offers.
The Queen of Sheba came to test Solomon with hard questions.
But now the greater King confronts us with a question no amount of wealth, influence, intelligence, or religious activity can answer for us.
What will you do with Jesus Christ?
Will you keep Him at a comfortable distance?
Will you admire Him without obeying Him?
Will you continue postponing the repentance you know is necessary?
Or will you surrender?
Maybe your prayer today does not need to be eloquent.
Maybe it needs to be honest.

“Lord Jesus, I have heard so much about You, but there are places in my heart I have kept closed. I have questions, wounds, fears, and sins I can no longer pretend are harmless. Forgive me. Teach me to trust Your Word. Turn my heart away from what dishonors You. Help me follow You, not merely speak about You. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I need Your grace. Change me from the inside out. Amen.”
These words are not a formula that earns salvation.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith.
But if that prayer expresses the sincere turning of your heart toward Him, do not let this moment disappear beneath the distractions of another ordinary day.
Open your Bible.
Read Matthew 12.
Read 1 Kings 10 and 11 together.
Notice both the splendor of Solomon's reign and the warning of his later compromise.
Then read the Gospels and behold the greater King.
And as you do, remember this:
The Queen of Sheba was willing to travel far to investigate the wisdom she had heard about.
You have the testimony of Jesus Christ preserved in Scripture within reach.
Do not allow familiarity to make you careless with such a gift.
And please, do not walk through this conviction alone.
You do not need to reveal private details to strangers. But sometimes an honest response becomes the beginning of encouragement, prayer, and genuine Christian fellowship.
And if this message brought someone to mind, do not ignore that person.
Perhaps it is a family member who has slowly drifted from church.
A friend who has become bitter toward God.
A believer who is quietly struggling.
A young person who knows Christian language but has never seriously examined the Gospel.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus came.
And if you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, consider joining this growing community of people who want more than occasional religious inspiration.
We want to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, discipleship, and a living relationship with Jesus Christ.
Because one of the greatest things we can offer another human being is not another argument to win.
It is an invitation to encounter the truth about Jesus.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another way to walk alongside this mission.
These resources are intended to nourish faith, encourage spiritual maturity, strengthen biblical understanding, and equip people to share the Gospel faithfully.
We believe the message of salvation must never be treated as something that can be purchased.
The grace of God is not for sale.
Prayer is not for sale.
Forgiveness is not for sale.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry of biblical teaching, free resources, and ongoing discipleship does require people who are willing and able to help.
Scripture teaches that believers may generously support those who labor in Gospel ministry (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14; 2 Corinthians 9:7).
But Scripture also teaches that giving should never be driven by guilt, compulsion, or the promise that God's favor can be bought.
If you have been looking for a practical way to help extend biblical encouragement beyond your own circle, this is one way to do it.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for reflection, and opportunities to encourage meaningful conversations about faith.
It is the people who may be reached.
The person who opens a devotional while struggling with despair.
The believer who returns to Scripture after years of spiritual neglect.
The family member who shares a Gospel message with someone who has stopped attending church.
The reader who discovers that Christianity is not about pretending to be righteous but about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
We cannot promise that every article will change a life.
Only God can bring spiritual life and lasting transformation.
But we can remain faithful in planting and watering, trusting Him for the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).
And perhaps your partnership can help place another faithful message within reach of someone who needs to hear it.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
And your love for Jesus cannot be measured by a monthly payment.
What matters is that Christ is honored, His Word is handled faithfully, and His Gospel is proclaimed.
Because this was never meant to be about building a platform greater than the message.
It is about using every opportunity entrusted to us to point beyond ourselves to the Savior.
Just as the Queen of Sheba looked beyond Solomon's splendor and blessed the LORD, may everything we do direct attention beyond Gospel Warrior to Jesus Christ.
The One who is greater than Solomon.
The One whose wisdom cannot fail.
The One whose righteousness is perfect.
The One who gave His life for sinners.
The One who rose victorious over death.
The One who calls the weary to Himself.
And the One who is worthy of our trust, our obedience, our worship, and our lives.
The Queen of Sheba came searching for answers and left astonished by the wisdom of a king.
But you are being invited to something greater than astonishment.
You are being called to faith.
To repentance.
To grace.
To a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And one day, when every earthly crown has lost its shine, every palace has turned to dust, and every human achievement has passed away, the glory of Jesus Christ will remain.
So do not spend your whole life admiring the wisdom of a lesser king while ignoring the Savior who stands above them all.
She traveled across kingdoms to hear a king's wisdom. The greater King came into our broken world to save sinners—and the question now is whether you will receive Him.
